newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bunds climbed high enough, must descend - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Bunds climbed high enough, must descend - analysts.

text.p: German Bunds, buoyed by news Bonn plans no further Bund issue this year, will not rise much further and will ease by year-end, analysts said on Thursday.
December Bund futures rose to a new contract high of 98.95 on the German DTB futures exchange, up 0.28 point on the day.
But analysts said the gains were mainly driven by futures trading and not backed up by heavy buying from investors.
The market had developed its own momentum after Wednesday's half-point jump caused by the U.S. Federal Reserves's decision to keep interest rates unchanged, they said.

But with the German economy gathering pace and prospects for another Bundesbank rate cut slim at best, there was no fundamental economic reason for 10-year Bund yields to be as low as their current level of 6.1 percent, analysts said.

In addition, sentiment could be dampened if the flaming row between unions and employers over the implementation of cuts in sick pay escalates into strikes, as threatened by banking and insurance union HBV on Thursday, analysts said.
Many top German companies including giant Daimler-Benz have announced they will cut sick pay from October 1.

That has fuelled a heated debate over whether the cut, part of new austerity legislation to boost employment and curb public spending, can be applied to existing wage contracts or just to newly negotiated ones.
"The long end of the German market is at a very exposed high," said Florian Staerk, bond analyst at Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG in Munich.

"German yields are practically at six percent. That's a level that in recent years we have only reached during extreme pessimism on the economy. Today, there is no more reason to be pessimistic than a few weeks or months ago."

The difference or spread between Bunds and Treasuries, at minus 69 after the release of U.S. durable goods orders on Thursday, was already too wide to be justified by economic fundamentals, analysts said.
Both Staerk and Karen Kricks-Brunnlieb, head of bond analysis at Trinkaus & Burkhardt, predicted Bund yields would rise to about 6.40 percent by the end of the year.
"It will be difficult for the Bund yield to fall below six percent," said Kricks-Brunnlieb.
Bunds received a boost after August U.S. durable goods orders tumbled 3.1 percent to post the sharpest fall in 16 months and reinforce the view the U.S. economy was slowing.

The data followed Thursday morning's announcement that the German government only planned to issue 6-month, two-year and five-year debt during the fourth quarter, but no 10-year or 30-year paper until early 1997. That helped nudge Bunds higher.
December Bunds cut gains in late afternoon trade and were quoted at 98.75 at 1415 GMT, up 0.08 point on the day.
Dealers and analysts did not rule out that Bunds may vault 99.00 but said any major push beyond that level was unlikely.

"We can crack 99. That's not a problem. But for that to be justified by fundamentals, we'd need negative news on the economy, and recent data has confirmed expectations for a pick-up in growth," Staerk said.
